ops.title: deploy cannot stop a daemon that fails Trust.Control, and the one-line settle routing that would fix it is unsafe
ops.description:
Investigated and **deliberately not landed**, 2026-08-30. The work exists unpushed on branch `untrusted-settle` (worktree `~/.claude/worktrees/daemonkit/untrusted-settle`, commit `7de9c01`); it is recorded here rather than shipped.

## The gap

`deploy/quiesce.go`, `(*Deployment).stop`:

    control, err := d.client.Control(ctx)
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, daemonkit.ErrDraining), errors.Is(err, daemonkit.ErrAbsent):
        return d.settle(ctx)
    case err != nil:
        return daemonkit.Stopped{}, err
    }

`ErrDraining` and `ErrAbsent` both mean "no usable control session" and fall back to the session-less `settle` arm. `daemonkit.ErrUntrusted` means the same thing but hits `case err != nil` and aborts. Every destructive verb funnels through here (`Quiesce` → `stop`; `Reset`, `Uninstall`, `Supersede` → `Quiesce`/`quiesceAndConverge`), so **a daemon that fails the deployment's `Trust.Control` requirement cannot be stopped, drained, or removed through the library at all** — including by `Reset`, whose own doc calls it "the way out of a state no other verb accepts". This is the failure that once drove a `rm -rf` of the state directory by hand.

## Why the obvious fix was rejected

Adding `ErrUntrusted` to the settle case is one line, and it does work: a real green→red→green bracket was cut (`TestStopSettlesAnUntrustedIncumbent`, RED on origin/main at `deploy_test.go:1202` with the trust error, GREEN after; `./scripts/test.sh -race ./deploy/...` green). An adversarial security review then found two CONFIRMED defects.

**1. It conflates two different refusals that share one sentinel.** `control.go:174-175` is the *client* refusing the serving peer — the in-scope case. But `control.go:215-216` maps a *server-side* authorization denial (`internal/wire/server.go:341-348`, the daemon refusing this caller's Control verb) onto the same `ErrUntrusted`. Routing it to settle turns a genuine authorization failure into an `ErrUnsettled` timeout, hiding it. Separating them needs a second sentinel or an `errors.As` on the wrapped cause — added machinery in the trust lane, for a narrow benefit.

**2. It widens a same-UID bypass past the inventory backstop.** `client.go:60-67` documents that the owner record is same-UID writable and that a forged record naming a dead PID yields a true `ReapAbsent` for a daemon still running. `requireEmpty` (`deploy/inventory.go:307-334`) attributes unnameable processes only against the *current* — i.e. forged — record, so the live incumbent is not flagged; `deploy/inventory_test.go:350-358` already demonstrates that class of husk clearing the gate. With the routing in place, an attacker who rebinds the socket (making the peer untrusted) and forges the record gets `deploy` to converge launchd empty against a live daemon — the exact irreversible step the `ErrUntrusted` abort was preventing.

## What the change would and would not have bought

Only the **husk** case: an incumbent recorded but already gone behind an untrusted socket occupant. A **live** untrusted daemon is unaffected either way — `Client.Settle` "dials nothing, sends nothing, and never signals", so `observeGone` simply runs out the deadline and returns `ErrUnsettled`. The change never makes a live untrusted daemon go away, because `quiesceAndConverge` deliberately never takes services from a runtime not yet proved absent.

## Operator recovery today, and it is adequate

End the process outside the library, then re-run the verb:

    launchctl bootout gui/$UID/<label>      # or kill the PID the owner record names
    <verb>                                  # Reset/Uninstall now settles the gone incumbent and proceeds

## Related

This is the residual behind the `ccp package reset` escape hatch: that verb reaches `deploy.Reset`, and `Reset` is subject to exactly this gate. The verb is still worth having — it is the way out of a sealed activation whose daemon restarted, a removal proof for an app put back by hand, or a plain file planted at a generation slot — but it is not a way past a live untrusted daemon.</body>

ops.text: Decide whether daemonkit.ErrUntrusted splits into a client-side 'I refuse this peer' and a server-side 'this peer refuses me', so the two can be routed differently
Decide whether deploy.requireEmpty attributes unnameable processes against something stronger than the same-UID-forgeable owner record

Once both are decided, a destructive verb against an untrusted-but-gone incumbent succeeds through the CLI, and against a live untrusted one fails with an error that names the trust refusal rather than a timeout
